# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–39 (Updated 2026-10-13, Final Revision 12)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of tenth year after Waterloo (1831). Story spans from Sunday, 26th April dinner (Chapters 1–35) through Chapter 36 (winter into summer) to Chapters 37–38 (spring/early summer) to **Chapters 39 (autumn)**. Emperor of China dinner scheduled Monday, 8th July; election for Westminster borough Tuesday, 9th July. Chapters 37–38 set in Harrowgate hill farms, coastal towns, Dunholt village, Staveton harbor town, transitions to London and Liverpool. **Chapter 39 set in village of Yarlton and London lodgings (Islington).**
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Bruton Street, Queen's Gate, Islington, City Road Music-Hall, Cannon Street Hotel, Euston Square, Liverpool); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Southend; Harrowgate; Lowestoft; Dunholt; Staveton; Gulton; Dunwick; Salford; Yarlton; coastal towns; rural areas (Sheep's Acre Farm, etc.).

## Major Deaths
John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt, Wevie Lindner (died winter, buried Salmere). Conar Hollett (drowned crossing estuary at Gulton; no body seen; Halan Hollett reported it at inn).

## Rebecca's Arc
Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon) receives allowance but refuses to see her. Appears wealthy at Bath/Cheltenham, busies herself with piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
Married at Ostend; Amelia initiated encounter. Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; daughter Jane his pride.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Welbeck Street resident. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review; praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" (Mr. Broune). Rejected Mr. Broune's proposal via letter; full of regrets; in debt. Overdrawing her account at bank. **A miserable woman—discovered Felix's failed elopement plan; helped him to bed early morning Wednesday after he arrived drunk at 6–7 A.M., fell in gutter, soiled and intoxicated.**

**Felix Carbury**: Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. **Chapter 38–39 (ELOPEMENT PLAN FAILED)**: Received £250 from Didon Monday 4 P.M.; understood he must go to New York. Planned passage Tuesday under name "Walter Jones," spend Tuesday with Ruby at Music Hall, depart Wednesday 5 P.M. for Liverpool. Attended Music Hall 10 P.M. to nearly midnight; Ruby did not appear; returned to club despite danger. Found Dolly Longestaffe and Miles Grendall; whispered to Grendall to convert I.O.U.s to cash; Grendall refused. Had been drinking freely; held up scraps of paper, asked loudly if any would buy for five shillings in pound. Called Grendall to card-room with Dolly as witness; Grendall again refused. **Played at Beargarden till 4 A.M.; intoxicated and almost penniless; made unpleasant remarks about Miles Grendall (accused of cheating at loo, appealing to Dolly as witness; claimed Grendall should be turned out of club); desperate row ensued; Dolly said he knew nothing about it; Lord Grasslough opined more than one person might be turned out. At 4 A.M. left club with only ten-pound note; all luggage left in hall. Between 6–7 A.M. knocked at Welbeck Street door; latch-key inefficient; door locked. Lady Carbury opened door; he was sodden with gutter, drunk. Lied claiming "old shap stopped ush" (Melmotte); Melmotte was actually asleep in Grosvenor Square, ignorant of plot. Felix stumbled upstairs; mother removed his clothes and boots; he fell asleep. Still in London as of Chapter 39.**

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit (too young, age disparity). Paul returned "as still dear friend" within week, promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. Roger declared love anew; determination unshaken. Paul thoroughly in love with her. Chapter 36: Paul visited her at Welbeck Street; she told mother loves someone else and praises Roger as "rock of strength."

## Marie Melmotte and Elopement Attempt

**Marie Melmotte**: **Chapter 38 (ELOPEMENT EXECUTED BUT INTERCEPTED)**: Sat up all night packing treasures with Didon; discussed American clergyman marrying them on board. Determined not to eat morning so no suspicion raised. **6 A.M. Wednesday: Robert departed first with big boxes (ten pounds in pocket). Marie and Didon followed in second cab with smaller luggage. Reached Euston Square without impediment; obtained tickets in French; got bad tea/uneatable food at station. Took seats without impediment; departed. As drew near Liverpool, Didon explained must not declare destination till ship at sea. Marie sure dangers over if only Felix safe on board. ELOPEMENT INTERCEPTED AT LIVERPOOL PLATFORM: Upon train arrival, gentleman (with another less-gentlemanly gentleman and nearby policeman) addressed her: "You, I think, are Miss Melmotte." Marie struck dumb. Didon immediately became voluble in French, claiming young lady was Mademoiselle Racine, her niece, she was Madame Racine, knew nothing of Melmottes. Gentleman insisted, used her English, named them both. Marie declared she spoke French; he countered "And English too." Gentleman told them to return to London; he would accompany them. Didon asserted legality of their position; had done nothing against laws. Gentleman spoke in low voice: cheque changed from father's house; father would pardon when she rejoined him; could arrest her on cheque if forced; certainly would not let her board. If she traveled back with him, no unnecessary inconvenience. Gentleman telegraphed Grosvenor Square during journey. At Euston Square met by one of Melmotte carriages. Marie taken home; boxes to follow at interval so Grosvenor Square might not appear aware (though it very soon knew all about it).** **Chapter 39: Marie aware she would be interrogated. Melmotte held her very hard, shook her while speaking, reminding her of his generosity (carriages, horses, bracelets, brooches, silks, gloves, everything else); declared "I've been very good to you." Marie shows determination: "I don't think that mamma cares. It's papa. I'd do it again to-morrow if I had the chance." She continued: "I would. Why is a girl to be made to marry to please any one but herself? I won't. And it's very mean saying that I stole the money. I always take what I want, and papa never says anything about it."**

## Didon
Marie's attendant. Executed elopement plan; presented Melmotte's cheque to bank, obtained £250, delivered to Felix at Beargarden Monday 4 P.M. Held tickets under name "Madame Racine." Departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with Marie in cab; faithful throughout; declared anxiety would not be over till ship moving. Intercepted at Liverpool; became voluble in French; asserted legality of position. To receive £50 before boarding (plan failed).

## Ruby Ruggles and Suitors

**Ruby Ruggles**: Pretty servant/maid to Mrs. Pipkin at Islington. Danced with Felix at City Road Music-Hall. When Felix refused marriage, Roger Carbury warned her forcefully; extracted promise not to see him again. Wrote Felix letter of regret; he replied tersely: Tuesday. Sought to attend Tuesday dance; Mrs. Pipkin refused, then reluctantly agreed. **Ruby attended Tuesday evening at Music Hall; Felix was there 10 P.M. to nearly midnight; did not connect (Felix noted her "non-appearance" and was "very angry"). Chapter 39: Second morning after night of imprisonment; nothing alleviated her woe. Her lover should have been in Liverpool but was abed in Welbeck Street. Ruby had written to Sir Felix the very night of her imprisonment but had not received reply. Opens door for Paul Montague; asks "Is Sir Felix still in London?" Greets Paul with unhappy countenance; holds baby in arms; little child (Sally) hanging on to her dress.**

**John Crumb**: Country lover from Suffolk, "Bungay mealman." Chapter 35: Attempted to take Ruby's hand; Ruby fled. Rode to Carbury Hall. Chapter 37: Visited Roger, expressed anguish about Felix, willingness to "swing for it" if seduced. Roger assured him Ruby good, promised Mrs. Pipkin supervision. Resolved to send Mrs. Pipkin price of new blue cloak via Mixet's letter and money order.

**Daniel Ruggles**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm. Violent; pulled Ruby by hair. Told Roger suitor should speak his mind.

**Mrs. Pipkin**: Ruby's aunt at Islington; lets lodgings. Feared Ruby would escape; reluctantly allowed Tuesday attendance at Music Hall. Chapter 39: Present in house when Paul visits. Present when Mrs. Hurtle announces departure; would have hysterics at Mrs. Hurtle leaving; found Mrs. Hurtle excellent lodger who never inquired about victuals, always suggested children eat the pudding or finish the pie, never questioned bills.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Crisis and Correspondence (Chapter 39)**: Returned to London Monday morning from Suffolk. Sat in his lodgings thinking of his condition; almost wished he had taken Melmotte's offer and gone to Mexico. Dreamed of life like Roger Carbury's—seemed far beyond reach. Wondered if he should go away, write to Hetta and bid her marry Roger. Mexico journey no longer open; had repudiated proposition and quarrelled with Melmotte. **Twice lately gone to Islington determined to see Mrs. Hurtle for last time. Took her to Lowestoft, equally firm in resolution to end bonds. Now promised to go again to Islington; aware if he failed she would come to him. No end to it.** **Wrote to Mrs. Hurtle: acknowledged circumstances made their lives and temperaments too different for happy marriage; fault was his; better to own fault and take consequences than marry with consciousness marriage would be sorrow and repentance. Confessed that had asked him if attached to another woman; answered truth but would not have spoken of altered affections of own accord. Broke engagement before knowing this girl; did not break because came to love her. No grounds for hoping love will lead to results. Told her condition of mind exactly. If possible would compensate injury or undergo retribution; could she exact? Thought further meeting avail nothing. But if she wishes, will come last time—because promised.**

**Mrs. Hurtle's Response and Chapter 39 Meeting**: **Letter duly reached Paul at his lodgings (Chapter 39). She suffered many injuries; this worst, most unpardonable, most unmanly. Called him coward, false liar. Poor wretch she destroyed was mad with liquor, acting after his kind. Even Caradoc Hurtle never premeditated such wrong. He bound himself by most solemn obligation joining man and woman together, then told her they go for nothing because do not suit his view. On thinking over, finds American wife would not make comfortable as English girl—therefore all to go for nothing! Has no brother, no man near her; or he would not dare. Called him coward. Talked of compensation; does he mean money? Insult more. As to retribution: yes. He shall suffer. Desires him to come to her according to promise; will find her with horsewhip in hand. Will whip him till has not breath in body. Then will see what he dares do—whether will drag her into court for assault. Yes; come. Shall come. Knows now welcome he shall find. Will buy whip while this reaching him; know how to choose such weapon. Calls upon him to come. Should he be afraid and break promise, she will come to him. Will make London too hot to hold him; if not find him will go with story to every friend he has.** **Paul started immediately for Islington upon receiving letter. Had no desire to delay meeting. Taught her his gentleness, going to play, drinking tea at Mrs. Pipkin's, journey to sea, were not evidence gradually being conquered. Declared purpose plainly at Lowestoft and in last letter. She told him at hotel, had she been armed by chance, would have shot him. Could arm herself now if pleased; his real fear not in that direction. Pang consisted in assuring her he resolved to do her wrong. Worst now over.**

**Chapter 39 Meeting Details**: Paul shown into Mrs. Hurtle's room. His mind altogether intent on his own troubles. Mrs. Hurtle very calm but quietness assumed; could convert into violence at any moment; her eye foretold spring of wild-cat. She pointed seat at distance from herself. **Paul sat. Mrs. Hurtle said his wishes do not affect her much. Asked if he thinks it best they never see each other again. She spoke softly: "Why should a gentleman trouble himself to say any more,--than that he has changed his mind? Why make a fuss about such little things as a woman's life, or a woman's heart?" She suggested he might say he is gentleman and man of his word, repents intended perfidy; might she not reply his hand could go where his heart gone, she scorned to be wife of man who did not want her?** 

**As she spoke she raised voice, half-lifted in seat, stretched toward him. He said nothing possible to answer.** **Mrs. Hurtle declared: "But I should not. I at least will be true. I should take you, Paul,--still take you; with a confidence that I should yet win you to me by my devotion. I have still some kindness of feeling towards you,--none to that woman who is I suppose younger than I, and gentler, and a maid." Asked advice what to do next. Has given up every friend for him. Has no home; Mrs. Pipkin's room more her home than any other spot. Has all world to choose from but no reason for choice. Has property. What shall she do with it? If could die and be no more heard of, Paul should be welcome to it. Asked: "You are in some degree responsible,--are you not,--for my loneliness?"** 

**Said she better remain here; does good to Mrs. Pipkin, who went into hysterics yesterday when Mrs. Hurtle spoke of leaving. Mrs. Pipkin would starve in America; Mrs. Hurtle desolate here. Then paused, absolute silence for minute.** **Asked if he thought her letter very short. Said no. Admitted had much more to say; that was third letter written. Had to choose which to send. His letter easier written; he had no doubts; she had many doubts.** **She handed him sheet containing threat of horsewhip. Then handed him scrap written at Lowestoft. She had thought of womanly weakness in soft moment; wrote other letter.** 

**She said: "Nay, I would not hurt you,--not at this moment. Sometimes I feel that I could tear you limb from limb, so great is my disappointment, so ungovernable my rage! Why,--why should I be such a victim? Why should life be an utter blank to me, while you have everything before you? There, you have seen them all. Which will you have?"** 

**Paul knelt. She said: "But it will be when you have left me;--and was when you were with me at the sea-side. And it was so I felt when I got your first letter in San Francisco. Why should you kneel there? You do not love me. A man should kneel to a woman for love, not for pardon." She put hand upon his forehead, pushed back his hair, looked into his face. Asked: "I wonder whether that other woman loves you. I do not want an answer, Paul. I suppose you had better go." Took his hand and pressed it to her breast. Asked: "Tell me one thing. When you spoke of--compensation, did you mean--money?"**

**After Paul left, Mrs. Hurtle rang bell for Ruby and asked Mrs. Pipkin to come. Announced standing upright in middle of room with smile on face: "Everything is over between me and Mr. Montague."** Mrs. Pipkin, prepared to have apron to eyes, asked if Mrs. Hurtle going to leave.

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman, South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway. Extremely busy with electioneering speeches, Committee members, dinner orders, commercial affairs. Told Felix entitled only to £600 shares now. Proposed Paul Mexican embassy; tone dubious to Paul. Expressed relief dinner would be over. Received Board meeting call; ran off to Cannon Street Hotel meeting. **Chapter 39: Fast asleep in Grosvenor Square Wednesday morning, altogether ignorant of elopement plot. Later interrogated Marie about cheque; held her very hard, shook her while reminding her of generosity.**

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no London expenses. Desires to sell Pickering, disembarrass Caversham. Dolly refused consent unless half produce given to him.

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Bruton Street rooms. Arrangement made: £5,000 pay off tradesmen's debts, leave him comfortably possessed; other £20,000 make property free. Returned demanding cheque on Melmotte's bank payable to his own. Has not received single ten-pound note. Threatens employment of Mr. Squercum if money not paid quickly. **Chapter 39: Present at club smoking-room Monday evening with Miles Grendall. When Felix accused Grendall of cheating at loo, appealed to Dolly as witness; Dolly said he knew nothing about it.**

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made protest against Melmottes. Following morning received invitation to stay with them. By Sunday present at Grosvenor Square.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City through New Mexico/Arizona into Mexico, terminating Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Stock at par; shares sold at premium. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not building railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury (now fled to America—or attempted to), Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty. Never owed shilling he couldn't pay. Firmly opposed Melmotte connection on principle. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless. Declared love to Henrietta anew; determination unshaken. Visited Ruby at Islington; warned her against Felix; extracted promise not to see him again; spoke to Mrs. Pipkin about late hours. Encountered Paul and Mrs. Hurtle at Lowestoft; greeted coldly; reproved Paul severely. Counselled marriage with her would be destruction. Upon Paul's return, expressed satisfaction: "Let her follow you, and bear it. Of course you must suffer the effects of your own imprudence."

## Minor Characters
**Lord Alfred Grendall**: Nearly overwhelmed by electioneering; nearly in rebellion. Burdened with seating arrangements.

**Miles Grendall**: Secretary to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour. **Present at club smoking-room Monday evening with Dolly. Felix whispered petition to convert I.O.U.s to cash; refused. Later when Felix accused him of cheating at loo and claimed should be turned out, desperate row ensued; Lord Grasslough opined perhaps more than one person ought turned out.**

**Robert** (servant): Marie's man; departed 6 A.M. Wednesday with big boxes, ten pounds in pocket; elopement intercepted.

**Yarlton Village and Surrounding (Chapter 39 backdrop)**: Village characters (Rira Stenworth, Colan Lindson, Wewyn Corrett, Cobin, Ilrine Corrett, Jotho Corrett, Ridette Lindson, Tassa) engaged in village life—mending sleeves, reading almanac, arguing over oats price, buying ribbon, moving to Mirecombe. Brenelle Brackwood left Dunwick, settled in Harrowgate. Road all ruts and puddles after thaw. Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Bell for vespers rang thinly. Light went early. River up again in spring. Wind off water smelled salt and tar. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Baker's boy late again, line at oven grew long. Rain threatening since morning but held off. Frost silvered hedges overnight. Children chased hoop down lane shrieking. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Dog barked at nothing and went quiet.

**Other Minor Characters**: Father John Barham (priest, Beccles); Sally Hockett (witnessed Daniel Ruggles pulling Ruby by hair); Mr. Squercum (lawyer threatened by Dolly); Caradoc Hurtle (Mrs. Hurtle's ex-husband, drunkard, scoundrel, divorced under Kansas law).
